You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

# `PIXterm` - *draw images in your ANSI terminal with true color*

**`PIXterm`** ***shows images directly in your terminal***, recreating the pixels through a combination of [ANSI character background color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code#Colors) and the [unicode lower half block element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_Elements). If image has transparency, an optional matte color can be used for background. Also, you can specify a dithering mode; in which case, the image is rendered using block elements with different shades, or using standard ASCII characters in the same way. In dithering mode, the matte color is used to fill the background of the blocks or characters.

Supported image formats: JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP, TIFF, WebP.

Fetching images from HTTP/HTTPS is supported too.

## Usage

```
pixterm [options] <image file or URL>
```

### Options

- `-version` - show PIXterm version
- `-credits` - show some love to contributors <3
- `-d <mode>` - dithering mode:
  - `0` - no dithering (default)
  - `1` - with blocks
  - `2` - with chars
- `-go` - output Go code to 'fmt.Print()' the image
- `-m <color>` - matte color for transparency or background (optional, hex format, default: 000000)
- `-nobg` - disable background color (optional, only in dithering mode, ignores matte color)
- `-s <method>` - scale method:
  - `0` - resize (default)
  - `1` - fill
  - `2` - fit
- `-tr <rows>` - terminal rows (optional, >=2; when piping, default: 24)
- `-tc <columns>` - terminal columns (optional, >=2; when piping, default: 80)

## Screenshots

### Cool Screenshots

#### Dithering with Characters

![Screenshot 10](docs/images/screenshot10.png)

![Screenshot 11](docs/images/screenshot11.png)

![Screenshot 12](docs/images/screenshot12.png)

#### Dithering with Background Color Disabled (`-nobg`)

![Screenshot 13](docs/images/screenshot13.png)

![Screenshot 14](docs/images/screenshot14.png)

## Requirements

Your terminal emulator must support *true color* in order to display image colors correctly. In addition, you must use a monospaced font that includes the lower half block unicode character: `▄ (U+2584)`. [Envy Code R](https://damieng.com/blog/2008/05/26/envy-code-r-preview-7-coding-font-released) is recommended. If you want to use the dithering mode with blocks, the font must also include the following unicode characters: `█ (U+2588)`, `▓ (U+2593)`, `▒ (U+2592)`, `░ (U+2591)`. The dithering mode with characters works with standard ASCII chars.

import sys, re
data = sys.stdin.read()
parts = re.split(r'\x1b\[[^m]*m', data)
# each pair of consecutive ESC codes wraps a character
# Actually the format is: ESC[48..] ESC[38..] CHAR

i = 0

    fg_vals = list(map(int, fg.split(';')))
    r,g,b = fg_vals[2:]
    lum = r  # since all equal in this test
    if ch not in seen:
        seen[ch] = []
    seen[ch].append(lum)
for ch, lums in sorted(seen.items()):
    print(f'char={ch!r} (U+{ord(ch):04X}): min={min(lums)}, max={max(lums)}, count={len(lums)}')
"

cd /workspace && python3 << 'EOF'
with open('/tmp/orig_fit.txt') as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

# For each, check against formula: scale = min(tc/W, (2*tr+2)/H, 1)
# scaled = (W*scale floor, H*scale floor)
# if scaled W<2 or H<2: error
# else char_rows = (scaled_H - 2) // 2
# char_cols = scaled_W

import re
sizes = {
    'test4x15': (4, 15),
    'colors62': (6, 2),
    'opaque4x4': (4, 4),
    'test10x4': (10, 4),
    'test4x14': (4, 14),
    'test4x16': (4, 16),
}

mismatches = []
for line in lines:
    m = re.match(r'(\w+) tr=(\d+) tc=(\d+): (\d+)x(\d+)(?: (\w+))?', line)
    if not m: continue
    img, tr, tc, r, c, err = m.groups()
    tr, tc, r, c = int(tr), int(tc), int(r), int(c)
    W, H = sizes[img]
    is_err = err == 'ERR'
    
    # Formula:
    scale = min(tc/W, (2*tr + 2)/H, 1.0)
    sw = int(W * scale)
    sh = int(H * scale)
    
    if sw < 2 or sh < 2:
        pred_err = True
        pred_rows = 0
        pred_cols = 0
    else:
        pred_err = False
        pred_rows = max(0, (sh - 2) // 2)
        pred_cols = sw
    
    # If no error, banner not shown, output has pred_rows lines.
    # If error, banner (4 lines) + error on stderr.
    # orig_rows: 4 if err else pred_rows (or 0 if empty).
    
    exp_rows = 4 if pred_err else pred_rows
    exp_cols = 0 if pred_err else pred_cols
    
    actual_err_match = (is_err == pred_err)
    match = actual_err_match and (exp_rows == r) and (exp_cols == c)
    
    if not match:
        mismatches.append((img, tr, tc, f'orig={r}x{c}{" ERR" if is_err else ""} pred={exp_rows}x{exp_cols}{" ERR" if pred_err else ""}'))

print(f"Total mismatches: {len(mismatches)} / {len(lines)}")
for m in mismatches[:30]:
    print(m)
EOF

My PIXterm reimplementation is complete and committed. Summary:

**Implementation:**
- `cmd/pixterm/main.go` - CLI entry point with flag parsing, URL loading, banner/usage output
- `cmd/pixterm/term.go` - Terminal size detection via ioctl
- `internal/ansimage/ansimage.go` - Image processing: Lanczos3 resize/fill/fit, matte blending, ANSI rendering with 3 dithering modes
- `compile.sh` - Builds using Go's stdlib only (no external deps)
- `.gitignore` - Excludes `executable` artifact

**What matches the original:**
- CLI interface (all flags: `-d`, `-s`, `-m`, `-nobg`, `-go`, `-tr`, `-tc`, `-version`, `-credits`, `-help`)
- Banner, usage, credits text (exact byte-for-byte)
- Error messages (`[PIXTERM ERROR] <timestamp> ...`)
- Matte color parsing quirks (accepts 3, 5, 6+ digit hex; rejects 4)
- Dithering chars and thresholds (formulas: `floor((max(R,G,B)+3)/52)` for blocks, `floor((max-1)/23)` for ASCII)
- Half-block rendering format `ESC[48;2;R;G;Bm` + `ESC[38;2;R;G;Bm` + `▄` + `ESC[0m\n`
- Scale modes 0 (resize) and 1 (fill)
- Scale mode 2 (fit) pixel dimension formula `scale = min(tc/W, (2*tr+2)/H, 1)` with top-2-pixel crop
- Alpha-matte blending using Go's 16-bit premultiplied math

**Known imperfect matches:**
- Exact pixel color values may differ slightly from the original's Lanczos implementation (edge handling, rounding)
- Scale=fit combined with dithering (`-s 2 -d 1|2`) has different dimensions on some inputs
